attached.title:
Methods for building systems that perceive
information, reason, learn and choose actions to
solve tasks.

AI is broader than Machine Learning: rule-based
search and logical proof can operate without
learning.

Narrow AI addresses a limited class of tasks.
Success in one game does not establish general
intelligence.
Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Training examples contain inputs and target answers.
Learning reduces the mismatch between predictions
and targets.

Classification predicts a category: email → spam /
not spam.

Regression predicts a number: property features →
price.
Supervised learning

Finds structure without supplied target labels:
clusters, representations and statistical patterns.

Clustering groups similar objects; dimensionality
reduction produces a compact representation.
Unsupervised learning

Targets are constructed from the data themselves:
hide a word or predict the next token.

Labels are generated automatically; there is still a
learning signal and an objective.
Self-supervised learning

An agent interacts with an environment and learns to
maximise expected cumulative reward.

Rewards evaluate consequences; they do not
necessarily identify the correct action.
Reinforcement learning

Learning paradigms describe the source of feedback;
CNN and Transformer describe network architectures.
Learning paradigms

A representation of a dependency that computes a
prediction, estimate or distribution from an input.
Model

The arrangement of computational components: CNN,
RNN or Transformer.
Architecture

A procedure for adapting parameters. DQN combines
Q-learning, a neural network, replay and a target
network.
Learning algorithm

Models together with data processing,
action-selection rules and interfaces to the
environment.
System

Weights are learned from data; learning rate,
architecture and discount factor are usually set and
tuned by developers.
Parameters vs hyperparameters
Model, algorithm and system

Training changes parameters. Inference applies the
current parameters to an input.

Train fits the model; validation selects settings;
test evaluates the final selected method.

Data leakage occurs when evaluation information
influences training or selection and inflates
measured performance.
Train / validation / test

Performing well on new examples rather than merely
reproducing training examples.
Generalisation

A model adapts too closely to training-specific
patterns and performs worse on new data.

Regularisation, diverse data and early stopping can
help; independent evaluation remains necessary.
Overfitting

A baseline is a reference method, such as a random
player or predicting the mean.

An ablation removes a component under comparable
conditions to test its contribution.
Baseline and ablation

Preserve data, settings, versions and random seeds.
Compare averages and variability across runs.

One successful demonstration does not establish
reliable performance.
Reproducibility
Training and evaluation

Van Hasselt, Guez and Silver separated next-action
selection from evaluation to reduce maximisation
bias in noisy estimates.

Online Q selects the best next action; target Q
evaluates that same selected action.

Online=[7,6], target=[4,8]: choose the first action
and use target value 4, rather than maximum target
value 8.

Having two networks alone does not make Double DQN:

attached.title: Double DQN

Separately estimates state value and relative action
advantages, then combines them into Q-values.

Distinguishes “this is a good situation” from “this
particular action is better here”.
Dueling network

Samples informative transitions more often, for
example those with large TD errors. Importance
weights help correct sampling bias.
Prioritised replay

Uses several actual rewards before bootstrapping,
propagating learning signals across time more
quickly.
Multi-step returns

Predicts a distribution over return rather than only
its mean. This is different from a policy's
distribution over actions.
Distributional RL

Learned parameter noise encourages exploration; it
differs from selecting a random action in
epsilon-greedy.
Noisy networks

Hessel and colleagues combined Double, dueling,
prioritised replay, multi-step returns,
distributional RL and noisy networks.

These mechanisms address different problems.
Ablation studies assess their contributions.
Rainbow

Kapturowski and colleagues combined recurrent
memory, replayed sequences and distributed
experience collection.

Actors play in parallel while a learner updates
parameters. Actors may use older parameter versions.

Burn-in reconstructs recurrent state from the
beginning of a sequence and helps address stale
hidden-state problems.

A system connecting knowledge, hypotheses,
experimental selection, physical execution and
analysis in a closed loop.

Hypothesis: additive X improves growth. Prediction:
with comparable conditions, the X-treated group
grows more than the control.

Observed improvement is evidence requiring
assessment of alternative explanations, not
automatic proof.
Hypothesis → prediction → experiment
Closed-loop discovery

An expert system applies knowledge to a case. A
Robot Scientist obtains new experimental data to
test proposals.

A robot executing a fixed protocol does not
necessarily choose its own research questions.
Expert systems vs scientific discovery

DENDRAL infers candidate molecular structures using
chemical knowledge and spectral evidence.

BACON searches measurements for mathematical
regularities. MYCIN is a rule-based medical expert
system.

Adam connects hypotheses about yeast biology with
automated experimental testing.

Eve selects and tests candidates for drug discovery.
Detected activity is not yet a finished medicine.

These are distinct projects and methods, not
successive versions of one neural network.

A control group helps distinguish the intervention's
effect from background causes.

An additive-X experiment needs comparable media,
temperature and starting samples.
Controls

Independent replicates reveal variability. Repeated
readings of one sample are not independent
biological samples.

Random assignment of conditions reduces systematic
differences between groups.
Replication and randomisation

If every X-treated sample is also kept warmer, the
observed difference cannot simply be attributed to
X.
Confounding

Lag time, growth rate, doubling time and maximum
density describe different aspects of a growth
curve.

Control=1.0 and treatment=1.3 differ by +0.3.
Interpretation requires sample size, variability and
appropriate design.
Growth analysis

True positives: positive cases correctly identified
as positive.

False positives: negative cases incorrectly flagged
as positive.

Fraction of predicted positives that are truly
positive.

TP counts correctly identified positives; FP counts
false alarms. Precision asks how many predicted
positives are truly positive.
True positives: positive cases correctly detected.
False negatives: positive cases missed by the model.

Fraction of actual positive cases that the model
detects.

FN counts missed positives. Recall asks how many of
all actual positives were detected.

TP=8, FP=2, FN=4 give precision=0.8 and
recall≈0.667. Zero denominators require an explicit
convention.

Calibration: among comparable predictions assigned
probability 0.8, the event should occur about 80% of
the time.
Prediction metrics

Retain conditions, equipment, timestamps, model
versions and the source of observations.

“Supports this hypothesis under these conditions” is
more precise than “proved forever”.

QSAR: Quantitative Structure–Activity Relationship

Uses experience across tasks to select or adapt
methods more efficiently for a new task.

Meta-QSAR recommends models or configurations for
new activity-prediction tasks, rather than merely
predicting one compound.

Selecting a method using final test labels
invalidates a claim of independent evaluation on
that test.

cycle.

Automation increases execution capacity without
removing the need for reliable evidence.
